title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

I'm your host, and over this series we're going to spend serious time with one of the great novels of the Victorian age — George Eliot's story of the Tulliver family, and of Maggie Tulliver in particular.
A novel about childhood, about the pull of the past, about what society does to people who don't quite fit its shape.
Joining me today are three people who know this book with real depth and real feeling, and who I suspect will not always agree with one another.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong reader of fiction as moral inquiry.
He reads Eliot with an eye for individual character — for goodness tested, for weakness of will — and he resists any reading that reduces the novel to a social programme.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows precisely what the institutions in this novel actually were — how the law worked, what debt meant, what it cost to be ruined.
He brings the real world to bear on Eliot's fictional one, and he's not afraid to get angry on behalf of people history forgot.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read The Mill on the Floss as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
She focuses on the experience of reading — what moves you, what makes you stop, what makes you want to read a sentence aloud to someone in the next room.

We begin today with the novel's shadow — the moral atmosphere Eliot creates, the weight she places on ordinary life, and the devastating force she can bring to bear on a single scene between a brother and sister.
James, I'd like to start with you, because Eliot opens her moral world with a provocation — an argument about how ordinary people do harm.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Eliot states her moral thesis — and how unsparing it is.
We tend to think of wickedness as deliberate — as scheming and plotting.
Eliot will have none of that.
She tells us that plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance are nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist.
And then she delivers the real indictment:

"It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations."
That list is devastating precisely because every item on it is so recognisable.
These are not the crimes of villains — they are the daily habits of ordinary, respectable people.
And that, I think, is precisely what makes the social world of this novel so suffocating.
I grant the passage its force — it's brilliantly observed.
But I'd resist the word suffocating, James — because Eliot's point isn't that the social world crushes people from the outside.
It's that we are all participants in that world — morally implicated by our own smallnesses.
The indictment falls on the self as much as on society.
And when you see that moral atmosphere made incarnate in a single scene, you feel the full weight of it.
Consider Tom and Maggie, when the family catastrophe first breaks over them.
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank, — as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
Tom holds Maggie — he does love her — and yet he cannot weep.
The rigidity is not cruelty, not yet — it is the first sign of what he will become.
That image — the black curtain falling — is doing an enormous amount of work.
Tom's inability to weep isn't just a psychological portrait — it's a social one.
He is a boy who has been taught to equate feeling with weakness, and duty with rigidity.
And that training — that very respectable, very English training — is what eventually makes him capable of the scene later in the novel that I find almost unbearable to read.
When Maggie returns after her time with Stephen Guest, Tom opens his mouth and what comes out is this:
"You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends.
You have been base, deceitful; no motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me."
That accumulation of second-person charges — you have, you have, you have — it reads like a verdict being read in a court.
And Tom believes he is being righteous.
He does believe it — and that is where Eliot is at her most uncomfortably honest.
Tom is not a hypocrite — he is something more troubling than a hypocrite.
He is a man who has mistaken his own hardness for virtue.
Eliot traced that particular confusion — I think — back to the very moment by the fire at school, when the black curtain fell and the tears would not come.
Caroline, you've been very patient — and I suspect you have something to say about both of those passages.
What do you make of Eliot's moral argument — and of Tom?
What I keep coming back to is the rhythm of Tom's speech in that scene — those repeated "you have" clauses.
It's percussive. It's punishing. It lands like blows.
And yet — and Edmund is right about this — Tom isn't raging for the pleasure of it.
He's trembling.
The text says he answers with tremulous rage — the trembling is still there, under the rigidity.
What Eliot is showing us is that the boy who could not weep has grown into a man who has channelled all that unexpressed feeling into moral condemnation.
And the Eliot passage James read earlier tells us exactly how that happens — not through dramatic villainy, but through accumulation.
Small omissions. Small rigidities. A curtain falling, year by year.
That's a thread we'll be pulling at throughout this series — how the novel traces the making of Tom Tulliver, and the unmaking of Maggie.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at the childhood world Eliot creates — the river, the mill, the family, and why the past holds such power in this book.
Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked — the programme where we slow down, go deep, and let George Eliot's great novel breathe.
Today's segment is called Maggie's Hunger: Education and Constraint.
We're asking what it meant for a girl of Maggie Tulliver's intelligence to grow up in a world that had no proper place for her.
With me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance — about goodness, weakness, and moral imagination.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about what the real world behind this fiction actually looked like.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been arguing with it ever since — in the best possible way.
Edmund, let's begin with you.
Eliot gives us Maggie Tulliver as a child of enormous inner life and very little outer scope.
What do you make of those childhood scenes — and what do they tell us about the character Eliot is constructing?
What strikes me first — and it never quite loses its force on re-reading — is the precision of the comedy.
Eliot is doing something technically audacious in that scene by the river.
She invokes the whole machinery of classical tragedy — the Greek requirement of magnitude — and then deflates it in a single sentence.
She writes, and I must read this precisely as she wrote it:

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action."
The Greek phrase is Aristotelian — the necessary greatness of action.
Eliot is saying: the passion is Lear's, but the action available to an eight-year-old girl in rural England is — pushing Lucy into the mud.
That gap — between the inner enormity and the outer impotence — is, I would argue, the novel's central tragedy.
And what I love — what makes me catch my breath even now — is the phrase Eliot uses for Lucy.
Not just Lucy — but "poor little pink-and-white Lucy."
That hyphenated description is doing so much work at once.
It's the colour of conventional feminine prettiness — the thing Maggie is not and can never be.
And the narrator's sympathy for Lucy — "poor little" — sits right next to the narrator's understanding of why Maggie did it.
That's the passage just before — where Eliot tells us Maggie was "actually beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or pinching her."
No sentimental evasion — Eliot shows us the ugliness of jealousy in a child, and doesn't flinch.
I want to come at this from the side of what Maggie's jealousy is actually about — because it's not simply about Tom's attention.
Eliot makes clear that it's about the withdrawal of the one domain in which Maggie had power.
She had been the one who "pet and made much of" Lucy — that was hers.
Now Tom has annexed even that small territory, simply by turning his attention toward it.
This is the structural reality of Maggie's childhood: she has no independent sphere — every space she inhabits is contingent on how the men around her are disposed.
That is well put, though I might resist the word "structural" — it risks making Eliot sound like a sociologist rather than a novelist.
What Eliot is showing us is something older and more permanent than any particular arrangement of society.
She is showing us what it is to have more nature than the world has room for.
That phrase — 'more nature than the world has room for' — takes us directly to what happens next.
After Tom and Lucy walk away, Maggie doesn't simply go home.
Caroline, she runs away to the gypsies — or tries to.
What does Eliot do with that fantasy?
It's one of the most beautiful comic-tragic sequences in the book — and that tonal balance is extraordinarily difficult to sustain.
Eliot shows us the resolution forming in Maggie's mind with perfect seriousness — she doesn't condescend to it.
The narrator tells us:
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark — that "No!" — is the whole of Maggie in one punctuation mark.
And then Eliot gives us the logic: Maggie had been told she was "like a gypsy" and "half wild" — so this is where she belongs.
She expects the gypsies will receive her with great respect, on account of her superior knowledge.
It's heartbreaking and hilarious in equal measure — and that's Eliot at her most generous.
And we get the narrator's gloss on exactly what kind of knowledge Maggie has — and hasn't — and it is devastating in its specificity.
Eliot writes that Maggie's mind contained:
"the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
She knew the word "polygamy" — she had deduced that "poly" means "many" — but she had no idea that gypsies were not well supplied with groceries.
The narrator calls her thoughts "the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams" — and that phrase is also, quietly, a diagnosis of what inadequate education produces.
She has read the dictionary — the dictionary, for want of anything better — and constructed a private cosmology from it.
One should be careful not to make too political a point of it — the comedy is also just splendidly funny.
Consider the gothic turn — the moment the fantasy collapses into something approaching genuine terror.
Eliot tells us that Maggie had begun to think — and I must read this — that the gypsies:
"meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — the specificity of that detail is pure Eliot.
It is the word of a mind that has read widely in mythology and fairy tale, and is now turning that reading upon its own predicament with terrible literalism.
And then there's the moment Eliot compares Maggie's theological curiosity to a professional theologian — and means it as no small compliment.
Maggie wonders "with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded" whether the Devil would know her thoughts.
She is eight years old, sitting in a gypsy camp, terrified, and still conducting a rigorous philosophical inquiry.
That is who Maggie Tulliver is — that is the whole problem of her life in miniature.
The problem of her life — and, as we'll see, the problem doesn't diminish with age.
Edmund, I want to bring in a passage from much later in the novel — the narrator's account of Tom Tulliver's mind.
Because it seems to me that Tom is, in some sense, the constraint that the title of our segment names.
It is one of the great passages of moral characterisation in the novel — and I think it deserves to be heard at length.
Eliot is writing about a certain kind of mind — not a wicked mind, mark you — but a mind that feeds on prejudice because it cannot feed on complexity.
She writes:
"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye, — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation."

"It is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton."
"A staff and a baton" — support and weapon simultaneously.
It is an act of extraordinary sympathy toward Tom, even as it convicts him utterly.
What strikes me about that passage is the word "bequeathed."
Tom's prejudice against Philip Wakem is literally inherited — bequeathed by his father along with the hatred of that family name.
Eliot makes this explicit — Tom holds himself "bound by his duty to his father's memory, and by every manly feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems."
That phrase — "every manly feeling" — is doing very sardonic work.
What Eliot calls a manly feeling is, in substance, the refusal to allow his sister a life.
And that is where the childhood passages and this one speak to each other across the whole length of the novel.
Maggie's hunger — her passion, her intelligence, her desire for something more — never changes.
But the constraint — which as a child was Tom's unkindness, Tom's indifference — hardens into something institutional.
It becomes Tom's authority over her choices, Tom's verdict on whom she may love.
The mud was always there — she's just no longer small enough to be pushed in it by accident.
That is a remarkable place to pause — and we will.
When we return, we'll be looking at what Eliot offers Maggie by way of consolation — or whether consolation is quite the right word.

segments.title: The Social Machinery: Class and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's great engines: the machinery of class, commerce, and financial ruin.
Mr Tulliver's catastrophe is not simply bad luck — it is a collision between pride, law, and the pitiless logic of provincial economy.
With me, as ever, are Sir Edmund Leigh, whose belief in the moral imagination keeps us honest about character over ideology.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who understands exactly what the institutions in this novel actually did to people.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt, whose close attention to the verbal texture of this novel never lets us forget that we are reading one of the great stylists in English.
Let's begin with the moment Tulliver's fate is sealed — and the narrator's astonishing choice of comparison for it.
The passage I keep returning to is the one where Tulliver's resolution — his firm determination to avoid Wakem's client — simply dissolves under the pressure of circumstance.
George Eliot tells us plainly that his will was not feeble — and that distinction matters enormously.
She is not writing a story about a weak man brought low by weakness.
She is writing about a man of genuine character ground down by what she calls — magnificently — external fact.
And then she reaches for Sophocles.
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
A provincial miller of the English Midlands set beside Sophocles' blinded king.
It ought to be presumptuous — and yet it is not, because George Eliot has earned it entirely.
What strikes me in that sentence is the absolute tonal control.
There is no irony at Tulliver's expense — which would be easy and rather cheap.
The narrator is genuinely indignant on his behalf.
And the comedy, when it comes, is aimed at the machinery, not the man.
Consider what happens just a few chapters earlier, when Tulliver writes that letter to Mrs Glegg.
The narrator sets up the comedy with such precision — Mrs Glegg sitting in her lofty magnanimity, anticipating reconciliation on her own terms.
And then the letter arrives.
He tells her the money will be repaid within a month, and that —
"he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
His pride is catastrophic and yet entirely comprehensible.
I want to anchor this in the legal and financial reality of early Victorian provincial life, because the comedy and the tragedy both depend on it.
Wakem is not a villain in any melodramatic sense — he is simply a competent attorney operating within a system that systematically advantages the legally literate over men like Tulliver.
Tulliver's description of him is wonderful in its revealing fury.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
What Tulliver cannot forgive is not malice — it is competence combined with implacable advantage.
And that is a far more honest account of how ruin actually works than most Victorian novels dare to give.
Blackstone is right about the legal texture, and I do not quarrel with it.
But I think what George Eliot is also doing — with rather more subtlety than is always credited — is tracing the interior logic by which a man defeats himself.
The passage about Mrs Tulliver's influence is devastating in its quiet precision.
The narrator tells us that Mrs Tulliver's pleading carried weight not because of her own personality, but because whenever she deviated from assent, Tulliver saw in her the entire Dodson family.
George Eliot's metaphor for this is exact to the point of comedy —
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
The blame, the narrator coolly insists, ought properly to lie with all the previous feathers — and that distributes responsibility with a philosophical rigour that Burke himself might have admired.
That metaphor is also very funny — genuinely, structurally funny — and I think the comedy is doing serious moral work.
Because it refuses to assign clean guilt.
No single person broke this family — it was the weight of accumulated pride, resentment, and small decisions, all pressing down together.
Which is why the tragedy in the next generation is so relentless.
Tom inherits all of it — the pride, the Dodson respectability, the determination to make the family name clean again — and turns it on Maggie.
His words to her are almost unbearable to read.

"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both."
He is not wrong, exactly — and that is what makes it so crushing.
Tom's demand that she swear on the Bible is worth pausing on — it is a legal instrument applied to a family relationship.
He requires the exact words of renunciation — not a promise, not an assurance, but a sworn formula.
He has learned, from his father's ruin, that informal trust is not enough — you need binding obligations.
And so the father's legal catastrophe reproduces itself as the son's moral tyranny over his sister.
The machinery grinds on through the generations.
I would resist framing Tom entirely as a product of social machinery — though I take Blackstone's point about the transmission of anxiety through the family.
Tom chooses this behaviour — he is not simply a mechanism.
George Eliot is always interested in the point at which circumstance becomes character — and Tom has hardened into something inflexible.
What saves the novel from determinism is Maggie herself.
Her battle with herself — which the narrator renders with extraordinary philosophical intensity — is genuinely free, genuinely moral.
She is not crushed by the machinery so much as she chooses — agonisingly — how to meet it.
That battle is rendered in one of the most extraordinary passages in the novel.
The narrator describes all the worst impulses surging up — the cruel selfishness, the sense of having been denied what others take freely.
And then against that surging, the old voices — conscience, memory, love.
And the image George Eliot finds for what it would cost Maggie to betray that conscience —
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
That word maiming — used twice, deliberately — is as precise and as shocking as anything in the novel.
And notice what Maggie is being asked to sacrifice — love, wealth, ease, refinement.

The narrator lists them as though taking an inventory — and every item on that list is something that would simply have been assumed for a young woman of her intelligence and feeling in a more equitable world.

The ruin that began with Mr Tulliver's pride and Wakem's legal advantage has flowed down to this — Maggie renouncing the life she deserves because the social order will not permit it to her on honest terms.
What we've traced, then, is ruin as inheritance — financial catastrophe hardening into moral tyranny, and moral tyranny pressing down on the one figure large enough to feel its full weight.
The machinery of class and commerce runs through this novel not as backdrop but as engine.
In our next segment we'll follow Maggie herself more closely — the interior life that the social world can constrain but never quite extinguish.

segments.title: Wit and Wound: Reading the Margins

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great architecture of this novel — its moral weight, its social machinery.
But this segment is about something more intimate: the wit in the margins, the tenderness in the detail, the sentences you stop and read again.
Caroline Woodcourt has been living with this novel since she was a teenager, and nobody notices what the prose is actually doing quite like she does.
Edmund Leigh brings his conviction that the novel's genius is finally moral — and he's never wrong about where the real life is.
And James Blackstone, who knows exactly what the world these children were born into actually cost.
Caroline — let's begin with the children.
What strikes me first about those early passages is how purely Eliot renders the sensation of not-yet-knowing.
Tom and Maggie are simply in their world — the mill, the Ripple, the great chestnut-tree — and they have no language for the fact that it will end.
The prose sets it up with such deceptive simplicity.
That word 'always' — repeated twice in one breath — is doing everything.
It isn't ironic on the surface; it's completely sincere, as a child is sincere.
And yet the reader already knows what the children cannot: that 'always' is exactly what won't be true.
One finds in that passage something that a lesser novelist would have sentimentalised into nothing.
Eliot keeps her irony entirely structural — it lives in the reader's knowledge, not in any authorial wink.
What I find equally remarkable is the passage about Tom's physiognomy just a little earlier.
Eliot is setting up the entire moral architecture of the novel in a meditation on a boy's unremarkable face.
She calls it the cunning of Nature — and then she delivers the sting.
That catalogue — rigid, inflexible, unmodifiable — is the sound of a door closing.
Tom's fate is announced in a description of his cheeks and eyebrows.
Yes — and what I love is the slight mischief in it.
Eliot calls Maggie 'the dark-eyed, demonstrative, rebellious girl' as though that's the conspicuous one to watch.
And then she quietly demolishes that expectation — the passive being may turn out to be Maggie after all, compared to this 'pink-and-white bit of masculinity.'
She's writing a comedy of false prophecy — and she's funnier about it than we sometimes admit.
That comedy has a harder edge when you consider what schooling actually was for a boy like Tom.
Stelling's curriculum — Latin supines, Euclid — was entirely disconnected from what a miller's son would need in the world.
It was a class performance, not an education.
And yet Eliot doesn't let that become a polemic.
She finds the scene's tenderness in this extraordinary moment where Tom resorts to prayer.
A twelve-year-old boy, whispering to God about Latin conjugations.
The comedy and the tragedy are inseparable — and that is Eliot at her most exact.
Inseparable — precisely the word.
Johnson said that the purpose of fiction is to instruct by pleasing; Eliot makes us feel the instruction before we can name it.
The cruelty of Tom's education is rendered comic — and then the comedy breaks your heart.
One notes that even in his prayer he is entirely practical: he asks God to make Mr Stelling say he shan't do Euclid any more.
That is Tom Tulliver perfectly caught — not the rigidity, not the cruelty, but the bewildered, earnest boy beneath.
And then there's Bob Jakin, who is an entirely different kind of comic creation.
Bob is performing — always performing — but there's a genuine intelligence in the performance.
In the scene with Mrs Glegg, he pitches his figured muslin by pretending to dismiss it entirely.
He says, with absolute deadpan confidence:
He's insulting her and flattering her and selling to her all in the same breath.
Eliot gives him the most alive vernacular prose in the book — every apostrophe, every dropped vowel earns its place.
Bob Jakin operates entirely outside the class anxieties that paralyse the Dodson women.
He's a pedlar — which meant, in this world, that he lived on his wits and his tongue.
Mrs Glegg has more capital but less cunning; Bob has everything to gain and nothing to lose — and the scene enacts exactly that asymmetry.
There's a sociology to the comedy that is as sharp as anything in the novel.
The comedy of the novel's society scenes reaches its most ferocious pitch in the St Ogg's passage after Maggie's return.
The narrator ventriloquises the town's gossip — and the mimicry is merciless.
One sentence in particular strikes me as among the finest pieces of satirical compression in the English novel.
How else, indeed.
The question mark in the middle of the sentence is doing tremendous work — it mimes the self-satisfaction of people who believe their moral shortcut is common sense.
And then she does something I find almost shocking in its boldness — she gives us the gossip at length.
She inhabits the collective voice of St Ogg's so completely that you almost can't find the narrator's own voice inside it.
She writes that public opinion, in these cases, is always of the feminine gender — not the world, but the world's wife.
That formulation is savage.
She's indicting not women but the enforced social role that makes women the vectors of judgment.
And notice how the passage ends — with Miss Unit refusing to visit Mrs Stephen Guest, and the crowd's verdict on her refusal.
The implication is that Miss Unit had no cards sent her — she's not punished for her virtue, she's simply excluded from the social game.
It's how conformity actually works — not through explicit coercion but through the withdrawal of ordinary social warmth.
Eliot understood that mechanism with the precision of someone who had lived it.
That's a thread running through everything we've touched today — the comedy that won't let you laugh without cost.
The happy morning that announces its own ending, the prayer about Latin, the gossip that does the work of a courtroom.
In our next segment, we'll follow that current deeper into the novel's moral heart — into the choices that define Maggie, and the world that offers her so few of them.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the deep currents of family life in Eliot's novel — the loves that form us and the fractures that follow.
In this segment we turn to the widening rift between Tom and Maggie Tulliver — and what Eliot says about the roots of belonging itself.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his unfailing attention to moral imagination and character — and I suspect he has strong views on what holds families together.
Professor James Blackstone is here as ever with the social and institutional backdrop — what it actually meant to grow up in that world.
And Caroline Woodcourt brings the reader's heart — the person who has lived inside this novel and knows exactly where it breaks you.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because Eliot opens this territory with a meditation on home and memory that I think is central to everything that follows.
Yes — and one must linger over it, because it is one of the most quietly radical passages Eliot ever wrote.
She is not simply describing Tom's happiness at coming home for the holidays.
She is making a philosophical argument — that affection precedes and defeats reason.
The passage I keep returning to runs as follows.

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
Before the labour of choice — that phrase is everything.
Eliot understands that the deepest attachments are not chosen — they are received, like one's own limbs.
And yet the novel then proceeds to show us how catastrophically those unchosen attachments can wound the people they bind together.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the way Eliot turns it on itself — she gives you the warmth and then she gently undermines it.
She says the familiar furniture would look very commonplace — even ugly — if put up to auction.
And of course that is precisely what happens to the Tulliver household.
The rug and the grate and the fire-irons — those beloved first ideas — are literally auctioned off.
Eliot plants the devastation right here in the pastoral warmth of Tom's homecoming.
That is why re-reading this novel is such a different experience — you see the traps being laid.
And there's a pointed social irony in the passage that I think is worth naming directly.
Eliot writes — with characteristic deadpan — about the striving after something better in our surroundings as the grand characteristic distinguishing the British man from the foreign brute.
That is a very sharp piece of satire aimed at the improving middle class — exactly the Dodsons.
The people who insist on better upholstery, better prospects, better marriages — and who have no patience for what cannot be made to show well.
Maggie, of course, can never show well in their terms.
Blackstone is right — but I'd add that Eliot is not simply satirising the Dodsons.
She understands them.
Their attachment to respectability is also a form of love — a very limited form, but rooted in the same deep soil.
What Eliot mourns is that the affections which ought to save us can also diminish us — or worse, diminish someone entirely dependent on them.
And that dependence falls most heavily on Maggie.
Caroline, there's a passage about Maggie's tears — her sense that the world is hard and unkind — that I think speaks directly to what Edmund is describing.
Oh, that passage — it destroys me every time.
Maggie has rushed upstairs to cry — because she cannot cry in front of her mother — and Eliot steps in with an observation that is almost unbearable in its precision.
She writes, and I want to read this slowly:

"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present."
The soul is made up of wants — not wisdom, not patience, not perspective — just wants.
And that is Maggie precisely — a creature of enormous appetite in a world that keeps reducing her rations.
But the cruelest thing is that last clause — we who looked on think lightly, as if our knowing the future somehow helps her in the present.
That address to the reader is a recurring move in the novel — and it has a very specific effect.
Eliot implicates us — she makes the comfortable reader complicit in the very condescension she's exposing.
We are the ones who think lightly of premature despair because we have the superadded life of experience and memory that Maggie lacks.
And the novel asks whether that superiority actually entitles us to anything — or whether it simply makes us more comfortable in our indifference.
What strikes me is how the passage connects Maggie's anguish specifically to the absence of love — not the absence of comfort or money.
Eliot writes that in books there were people who showed their kindness not by finding fault.
And Maggie's world outside books is precisely the opposite — affection expressed as criticism, as fault-finding, as disappointment.
This is the paradox at the heart of the novel's family life — love exists but it cannot be properly given or received.
And Eliot traces that failure with a sympathy that extends even to those — like Tom — who are doing the wounding.
Which brings us to Tom himself — and what Eliot reveals when Maggie is sent away from his school.
James, you've been looking at that passage about Tom's lessons — and what Maggie's presence actually did for him.
It's a beautifully observed passage — and it tells us something important about how Eliot construes intelligence.
Tom has been grinding through Stelling's curriculum — Latin grammar, Euclid — a curriculum designed for quite a different kind of mind.
Maggie arrives and simply asks the questions Tom has never thought to ask.
And the result, as Eliot puts it — and this is wonderfully comic:

"Tom had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
A dim understanding — not a revelation, not a transformation — a dim understanding.
Eliot is exquisitely fair to Tom here — she doesn't mock him, she simply measures the exact reach of what he can grasp.
And then he misses her grievously — that word is so carefully chosen.
Not sadly, not wistfully — grievously.
There is a genuine grief in Tom for Maggie's absence that he himself couldn't articulate.
He had really been brighter — Eliot says — since she had been there.
And yet when he is with her later in life, he cannot find a way to treat her well.
That gap — between what he feels and what he's able to give — is Tom's tragedy in miniature.
That observation about Tom opens onto the other passage I was asked to consider — the moment Maggie sees her father's helplessness.
Eliot here describes something she calls the supreme moment — when all we have hoped or delighted in falls away as insignificant.
And it is lost — her phrase — like a trivial memory, in what she calls:
"that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
Simple and primitive — that is not a diminishment in Eliot's vocabulary.
It is the bedrock.
And it is precisely this love — not reason, not ambition, not even justice — that governs Maggie's every decision.
And that is what makes the family's destruction so devastating — it is not simply material ruin.
When Tulliver says to his wife — and this is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the novel:
"we shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me" —
he is not speaking only of bankruptcy.
He is speaking of the exhaustion of a man who has been comprehensively defeated by forces he could never have named — legal, economic, social.
And his children must now carry the weight of that defeat — each in their own way, each bearing it badly.
What that line does — this world's been too many for me — is it strips away all of Tulliver's bluster.
Throughout the novel he has raged and litigated and blustered — convinced the world is against him personally.
And then in that one sentence he admits it: the world was too many for him.
Not Wakem, not fate — the world.
And he asks for a kiss.
That is the whole of the Tulliver family in one exchange — anger, helplessness, and a love that never quite knew how to show itself.
Burke wrote that the social bonds we inherit are more binding than any we could rationally construct.
Eliot is doing something similar — but she refuses Burke's optimism.
She sees the same deep bonds — the elderberry bush, the pattern of the rug — and she shows how they can become a prison as readily as a sanctuary.
Maggie is bound to this family by love she cannot escape — and the family, by its own limitations, cannot receive what she needs to give.
A prison as readily as a sanctuary — that is a wonderful way to hold the novel's central tension.
We'll be returning to where that tension leads — for Maggie and for Tom — in our next segment.
For now, thank you all — Edmund, James, Caroline — for a conversation that has, as ever, made the familiar pages feel entirely new.

segments.title: The Currents Converge: Narrative and Fate

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been moving through Eliot's novel with close attention to its craft, and now we arrive at something quite extraordinary — the question of how the story reaches us at all.

The opening of The Mill on the Floss does something audacious — it gives us a narrator who is herself dreaming, pressing her elbows into an armchair, and only gradually remembering that she has a story to tell.
And then, much later, there's a scene of extraordinary tenderness — Mr Tulliver on horseback, turning back because he cannot quite ride away from the thought of his daughter.
Edmund, Caroline, and James are all here, and I want to begin with that strange, self-conscious opening — with the narrator waking from her own reverie.

What strikes me immediately about that passage is its sheer confidence — the confidence of a novelist who knows she can stop the forward motion of fiction and invite the reader to notice the machinery.
Eliot sets up a narrator who is, in every practical sense, dozing in a chair — and then turns that dozing into a meditation on the nature of memory itself.
The passage reads, if I may —

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
That word "benumbed" — it isn't decorative.
It tells us that memory has a physical cost — that to inhabit the past fully enough to narrate it is, in some sense, to be temporarily stranded there.
Yes — and there's something almost comic about it too, which I think is important.
The narrator catches herself mid-dream, slightly embarrassed, rubbing her arms back to life — and then immediately says, in effect, "Never mind, here is what I was going to tell you."
It has the warmth of someone telling a story at a fireside — human, fallible, present.
What moves me is the phrase "many years ago."
Those three words do enormous work — they locate the narrator at a great distance from the scene she is about to conjure, and they make that distance feel like loss.
I'd add a layer to that — the physical specificity here is doing something historically precise.
Dorlcote Mill on a February afternoon is not a vague pastoral backdrop — it is a place in decline, in a season that is cold and unforgiving, rendered in the particular light of memory.
The narrator's reverie is the vehicle by which we are delivered into a world that is already, from the outset, under threat of disappearing.
That matters enormously if you want to understand why the novel's catastrophe feels inevitable rather than contrived.
Blackstone is right about inevitability, and it connects, I think, to the later passage — Mr Tulliver on horseback, turning back.
What Eliot does there is morally precise in a way that only the greatest novelists achieve.
She writes of Tulliver that — and I quote —
"He turned his head from side to side in a melancholy way, as if he were looking at some painful object on more sides than one."
"On more sides than one" — that is an extraordinary phrase.
It tells us that Tulliver's grief is not simple — it is the grief of a man who can see, from multiple angles, how badly the world is arranged for his daughter.
That phrase stops me every time I re-read it.
And then Eliot gives us those five words spoken aloud — the only thing Tulliver says in the whole scene.
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
"Belike" — that dialect word — is doing so much.
It's uncertainty — "perhaps," "probably" — and it shows that even in his most tender moment, Tulliver cannot quite trust Tom to be enough for Maggie.
He loves her, he fears for her, and he cannot fix it — all in a single breath.
That word "belike" also marks the limits of his world — he is a man of uncertain speech and uncertain prospects, and he knows it.

What the law would have told Mr Tulliver, had he thought to consult it, is that Maggie had essentially no independent standing — as a daughter, later as an unmarried woman, she was legally invisible in any number of crucial respects.
His anxiety on horseback is not sentiment — it is an accurate reading of the situation.
And Eliot understands this perfectly — she gives us a man who intuits structural injustice without having the vocabulary to name it.
I wouldn't quarrel with that — though I'd insist the power of the scene is not diminished by framing it as institutional critique.
Eliot says of Tulliver, remember, that he was "relapsing into the sense that this is a puzzling world."
"Relapsing into the sense that this is a puzzling world."
That word "relapsing" is magnificent — it tells us this is not a new thought, but an old sorrow returning, like a chronic illness.
The world puzzles Tulliver morally, not merely materially — and that is the heart of his tragedy.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is how these two passages bracket each other — the narrator who cannot quite leave her dream, and the father who cannot quite ride away.
Both are held in place by love — and by the knowledge that what is loved is already, in some sense, slipping away.
In our next segment, we'll follow the current forward — into the choices that Maggie and Tom make, and what the novel asks us to feel about them.
We've spent this episode tracing the lives of people caught between what they feel and what the world permits them to feel.
Mr Tulliver's impulsive pride, Maggie's moral seriousness, the institutions that grind people down without ever meaning to be cruel.
So for this final segment, I want to ask each of you the same question.
What does The Mill on the Floss leave us with — what is its lasting lesson, if a novel as honest as this one can be said to teach anything at all?
Sir Edmund, let's begin with you.
What the novel teaches — if we must use that word — is something deeply unfashionable.
It teaches that character is fate, and that the most devastating defeats are self-inflicted.
Consider Mr Tulliver.
George Eliot gives us one of her most precise diagnoses of a certain kind of ruin in that passage about his impulsive decisiveness.
She writes, and I think this is the sentence that rewards the slowest possible reading,
"for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread."
That is not satire at a safe distance — that is a portrait of every man who has ever convinced himself that urgency is wisdom.
And of course, the mill itself is lost, precisely because of such a snatch at a single thread.
I'd add only that George Eliot is careful not to let the individual carry all the weight of that diagnosis.
Tulliver's flaw is real — Edmund is right about that — but the system around him is perfectly designed to punish exactly that kind of flaw and no other.
A man of wealth could snatch at any number of threads and be insulated from the consequences by capital.
What the novel teaches me — as a historian — is that moral failure and structural failure are not opposites.
They operate simultaneously, and the honest novelist shows you both at once, without resolving the tension between them.
For me, what the novel ultimately teaches is something about the cost of conscience.
There's a moment near the end — Dr Kenn, alone, wrestling with whether to advise Maggie — that I find almost unbearably true.
He arrives at this conclusion about her — and the novel seems to arrive at it too —
"her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
That's the novel's deepest conviction — that there is something in a person that must not be argued out of itself, even when argument seems to be winning.
Maggie doesn't get rescued by the plot.
But her integrity is never forfeit — and the novel insists that is not nothing.
I confess I find that deeply moving — though I'd phrase the lesson rather differently.
There's a line Tulliver speaks to Maggie — just six words, and they contain everything the novel knows about time and regret.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
That is the Mill on the Floss, in a sentence.
Not a programme for reform, not a thesis about society — but a recognition that life, once squandered, is simply gone.
And that is worth any number of manifestos.
I won't quarrel with that — though I'd say the manifesto and the lamentation can coexist.
George Eliot doesn't sentimentalise Tulliver's regret — she shows you exactly how he arrived at it, thread by ill-judged thread.
And that insistence on showing the mechanism — not just the suffering — is what makes this a novel rather than an elegy.
A novel, not an elegy — though one that earns its grief honestly.
Character and fate, conscience and consequence, the skein we tangle and the life we can't live twice — it's all here.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done justice to a very great book.

The Mill on the Floss remains — more than a century and a half after its first publication — one of the most honest accounts of what it costs to live with integrity in a world that has other plans for you.
We hope you'll read it, or read it again.
Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c3:p79.text:
Plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance, in order to compass a selfish
end, are nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist: they demand too
intense a mental action for many of our fellow-parishioners to be guilty of
them. It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so
much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial
falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by
small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised
insinuations. We live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of
immediate desires; we do little else than snatch a morsel to satisfy the hungry
brood, rarely thinking of seed-corn or the next year’s crop.
c3:p79.summary: The narrator offers profound reflection that most moral failures result not from deliberate villainy but from small, thoughtless acts, lazy compliance, and accumulated minor dishonestries.
c3:p79.best_quote: It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations

c20:p31.text:
With these last words, Maggie’s sobs burst forth with the more violence
for the previous struggle against them. Tom felt that pressure of the heart
which forbids tears; he had no distinct vision of their troubles as Maggie had,
who had been at home; he only felt the crushing weight of what seemed
unmitigated misfortune. He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie
as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank,—as
if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path.
c20:p31.summary: Maggie's suppressed sobs burst forth violently, while Tom, feeling the crushing weight of misfortune, cannot weep; his face becomes rigid and his eyes blank.
c20:p31.best_quote: He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank,—as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path.

c54:p7.text:
“You will find no home with me,” he answered, with tremulous rage.
“You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father’s name.
You have been a curse to your best friends. You have been base, deceitful; no
motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You
don’t belong to me.”
c54:p7.summary: Tom delivers a scathing rejection of Maggie, condemning her as a curse on the family and declaring her no longer his sister.
c54:p7.best_quote: You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends. You have been base, deceitful; no motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me.

c10:p15.text:
There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if
tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι
μέγεθος which was present in the passion
was wanting to the action; the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of
her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the
cow-trodden mud.
c10:p15.summary: Maggie, consumed by conflicting passions, pushes Lucy into the mud—a small but consequential act that demonstrates the gap between inner tempest and outer deed.
c10:p15.best_quote: There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action; the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud.

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c51:p29.text:
But to minds strongly marked by the positive and negative qualities that create
severity,—strength of will, conscious rectitude of purpose, narrowness of
imagination and intellect, great power of self-control, and a disposition to
exert control over others,—prejudices come as the natural food of
tendencies which can get no sustenance out of that complex, fragmentary,
doubt-provoking knowledge which we call truth. Let a prejudice be bequeathed,
carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the
eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is
something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of
spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of
conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton. Every prejudice that will
answer these purposes is self-evident. Our good, upright Tom Tulliver’s
mind was of this class; his inward criticism of his father’s faults did
not prevent him from adopting his father’s prejudice; it was a prejudice
against a man of lax principle and lax life, and it was a meeting-point for all
the disappointed feelings of family and personal pride. Other feelings added
their force to produce Tom’s bitter repugnance to Philip, and to
Maggie’s union with him; and notwithstanding Lucy’s power over her
strong-willed cousin, she got nothing but a cold refusal ever to sanction such
a marriage; “but of course Maggie could do as she liked,—she had
declared her determination to be independent. For Tom’s part, he held
himself bound by his duty to his father’s memory, and by every manly
feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems.”
c51:p29.summary: The narrator characterizes Tom's mind as rigid and wedded to inherited prejudice; his narrow imagination and strong will make him incapable of questioning paternal grievances or considering Maggie's happiness with Philip.
c51:p29.best_quote: Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right

c13:p11.text:
Mr Tulliver’s prompt procedure entailed on him further promptitude in
finding the convenient person who was desirous of lending five hundred pounds
on bond. “It must be no client of Wakem’s,” he said to
himself; and yet at the end of a fortnight it turned out to the contrary; not
because Mr Tulliver’s will was feeble, but because external fact was
stronger. Wakem’s client was the only convenient person to be found. Mr
Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like
Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him.
c13:p11.summary: Mr Tulliver's search for a five hundred pound loan ends in ironic necessity: Wakem's client is the only available lender, presenting the narrator's philosophical reflection on Mr Tulliver as a man subject to tragic destiny.
c13:p11.best_quote: Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him.

c13:p5.text:
Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I
leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
c13:p5.summary: Mr Tulliver writes to Mrs Glegg announcing he will repay her five hundred pounds within a month and neither desires nor requires her favours, completely inverting her anticipated reconciliation.
c13:p5.best_quote: she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”
c37:p53.summary: Tom insists Maggie must put her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words of renunciation, claiming he cannot trust her, that she lacks consistency, and that while he has been working to pay their father's debts and restore family respectability, she has done everything to destroy both.
c37:p53.best_quote: I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both

c52:p2.text:
Maggie, all this time, moved about with a quiescence and even torpor of manner,
so contrasted with her usual fitful brightness and ardor, that Lucy would have
had to seek some other cause for such a change, if she had not been convinced
that the position in which Maggie stood between Philip and her brother, and the
prospect of her self-imposed wearisome banishment, were quite enough to account
for a large amount of depression. But under this torpor there was a fierce
battle of emotions, such as Maggie in all her life of struggle had never known
or foreboded; it seemed to her as if all the worst evil in her had lain in
ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous,
overpowering strength! There were moments in which a cruel selfishness seemed
to be getting possession of her; why should not Lucy, why should not Philip,
suffer?  She  had had to suffer through many years of her life; and who
had renounced anything for her? And when something like that fulness of
existence—love, wealth, ease, refinement, all that her nature
craved—was brought within her reach, why was she to forego it, that
another might have it,—another, who perhaps needed it less? But amidst
all this new passionate tumult there were the old voices making themselves
heard with rising power, till, from time to time, the tumult seemed quelled.
 Was  that existence which tempted her the full existence she dreamed?
Where, then, would be all the memories of early striving; all the deep pity for
another’s pain, which had been nurtured in her through years of affection
and hardship; all the divine presentiment of something higher than mere
personal enjoyment, which had made the sacredness of life? She might as well
hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in
which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs
of her soul. And then, if pain were so hard to  her , what was it to
others? “Ah, God! preserve me from inflicting—give me strength to
bear it.” How had she sunk into this struggle with a temptation that she
would once have thought herself as secure from as from deliberate crime? When
was that first hateful moment in which she had been conscious of a feeling that
clashed with her truth, affection, and gratitude, and had not shaken it from
her with horror, as if it had been a loathsome thing? And yet, since this
strange, sweet, subduing influence did not, should not, conquer
her,—since it was to remain simply her own suffering,—her mind was
meeting Stephen’s in that thought of his, that they might still snatch
moments of mute confession before the parting came. For was not he suffering
too? She saw it daily—saw it in the sickened look of fatigue with which,
as soon as he was not compelled to exert himself, he relapsed into indifference
toward everything but the possibility of watching her. Could she refuse
sometimes to answer that beseeching look which she felt to be following her
like a low murmur of love and pain? She refused it less and less, till at last
the evening for them both was sometimes made of a moment’s mutual gaze;
they thought of it till it came, and when it had come, they thought of nothing
else.
c52:p2.summary: Maggie experiences an unprecedented internal battle between cruel selfish impulses and her moral conscience, as the narrator reveals her struggle between personal happiness and loyalty to Lucy and Philip through a passage of intense philosophical introspection.
c52:p2.best_quote: "She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."

c5:p78.text:
It was one of their happy mornings. They trotted along and sat down together,
with no thought that life would ever change much for them; they would only get
bigger and not go to school, and it would always be like the holidays; they
would always live together and be fond of each other. And the mill with its
booming; the great chestnut-tree under which they played at houses; their own
little river, the Ripple, where the banks seemed like home, and Tom was always
seeing the water-rats, while Maggie gathered the purple plumy tops of the
reeds, which she forgot and dropped afterward; above all, the great Floss,
along which they wandered with a sense of travel, to see the rushing
spring-tide, the awful Eagre, come up like a hungry monster, or to see the
Great Ash which had once wailed and groaned like a man, these things would
always be just the same to them. Tom thought people were at a disadvantage who
lived on any other spot of the globe; and Maggie, when she read about
Christiana passing “the river over which there is no bridge,”
always saw the Floss between the green pastures by the Great Ash.
c5:p78.summary: The children imagine their happiness is eternal and unchanging; they associate the River Floss, the mill, and the landscape with home and permanence.

c5:p3.text:
Nevertheless he submitted to be kissed willingly enough, though Maggie hung on
his neck in rather a strangling fashion, while his blue-gray eyes wandered
toward the croft and the lambs and the river, where he promised himself that he
would begin to fish the first thing to-morrow morning. He was one of those lads
that grow everywhere in England, and at twelve or thirteen years of age look as
much alike as goslings,—a lad with light-brown hair, cheeks of cream and
roses, full lips, indeterminate nose and eyebrows,—a physiognomy in which
it seems impossible to discern anything but the generic character to boyhood;
as different as possible from poor Maggie’s phiz, which Nature seemed to
have moulded and coloured with the most decided intention. But that same Nature
has the deep cunning which hides itself under the appearance of openness, so
that simple people think they can see through her quite well, and all the while
she is secretly preparing a refutation of their confident prophecies. Under
these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she
conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most
unmodifiable characters; and the dark-eyed, demonstrative, rebellious girl may
after all turn out to be a passive being compared with this pink-and-white bit
of masculinity with the indeterminate features.
c5:p3.summary: The narrator reflects on Tom's ordinary boyish appearance contrasted with Maggie's distinctive features, suggesting that Nature hides immutable character beneath superficial appearances.

c14:p11.text:
Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”
c14:p11.summary: Humiliated by repeated failures, Tom resorts to prayer, adding petitions for Latin and Euclid to his nightly prayers, showing his desperation and underlying sensitivity.
c14:p11.best_quote: and please to make me always remember my Latin

“Eh, mum, I told you how it ’ud be,” said Bob, flinging aside
the coloured things with an air of desperation. “I knowed it ud’
turn again’ you to look at such paltry articles as I carry. Here’s
a piece o’ figured muslin now, what’s the use o’ you
lookin’ at it? You might as well look at poor folks’s victual, mum;
it ’ud on’y take away your appetite. There’s a yard i’
the middle on’t as the pattern’s all missed,—lors, why,
it’s a muslin as the Princess Victoree might ha’ wore; but,”
added Bob, flinging it behind him on to the turf, as if to save Mrs
Glegg’s eyes, “it’ll be bought up by the huckster’s
wife at Fibb’s End,—that’s where  it’ll 
go—ten shillin’ for the whole lot—ten yards, countin’
the damaged un—five-an’-twenty shillin’ ’ud ha’
been the price, not a penny less. But I’ll say no more, mum; it’s
nothing to you, a piece o’ muslin like that; you can afford to pay three
times the money for a thing as isn’t half so good. It’s nets
 you  talked on; well, I’ve got a piece as ’ull serve you to
make fun on——”
